title: Buran (commander's station)

sources.title: JoyPro cockpit catalog (panels, items and grip functions of the variant)

intro: Buran was the Soviet reusable orbiter, similar in shape to the American Space Shuttle. It flew only once, in November 1988, without a crew: its computers launched it, flew two orbits and landed it on a runway by themselves. The flight deck was built for a commander and a pilot side by side, with sticks, pedals, a translation controller and three screens, plus stations behind for an engineer and a robot arm operator. The controls are inferred from the labels of a cockpit diagram, so this guide says little about them.

panels.name: Dashboard with three CRT displays
panels.text: The front panel of the flight deck with three screens and flight instruments.
panels.context: It was laid out for a crew, but Buran's only flight was flown by its computers alone.

controls.name: CRT displays
controls.text: Three tube screens (CRT) that show the flight and the systems.
controls.context: They are the information display system of the flight deck.

controls.name: Flight instruments
controls.text: Instruments for the attitude (which way the orbiter points) and the speed.
controls.context: They would have been the commander's main instruments for the landing glide.

areas.name: Side desks
areas.text: The commander's and pilot's side desks.

panels.name: Left and right desks
panels.text: The side desks of the commander and the pilot with system switches.
panels.context: JoyPro infers them from a labelled cockpit diagram; their switches are not described.

controls.name: Commander's side desk
controls.text: The desk at the commander's side with switches for the systems.
controls.context: JoyPro's sources do not describe its single switches.

controls.name: Pilot's side desk
controls.text: The desk at the pilot's side with switches for the systems.
controls.context: JoyPro's sources do not describe its single switches.

panels.name: Central desk
panels.text: The desk between the two seats with shared controls.
panels.context: Both pilots would have reached it.

controls.name: Shared controls
controls.text: Controls between the seats that both the commander and the pilot can use.
controls.context: JoyPro's sources do not describe its single switches.

panels.name: Flight engineer and RMS stations
panels.text: Further stations behind the two pilot seats.
panels.context: Like the American Shuttle, Buran was planned with stations for an engineer and for a robot arm.

controls.name: Flight engineer station
controls.text: A station behind the pilots for a flight engineer who watches the systems.
controls.context: JoyPro's sources do not describe its single switches.

controls.name: Manipulator desk
controls.text: A desk with the controls of a robot arm for moving cargo in the payload bay.
controls.context: JoyPro's sources do not describe its single switches.

panels.name: Control stick
panels.text: The stick in front of the commander's seat.
panels.context: It would have flown the orbiter by hand.

controls.name: Control stick
controls.text: Moving the stick forward or back pitches the orbiter, sideways rolls it.
controls.context: Buran never flew with a crew, so this stick was never used in space; on a joystick it is the X and Y axes.

panels.name: Translation controller (controller block)
panels.text: A controller block next to the commander's seat.
panels.context: It would have moved the orbiter in orbit without turning it.

controls.name: Translation controller
controls.text: This controller moves the whole orbiter forward, back, left, right, up or down by firing its steering jets (translation).
controls.context: It was meant for meeting and docking with a space station.

panels.name: Pedals
panels.text: The rudder pedals at the commander's feet.
panels.context: They work only in the air, for the landing.

controls.name: Pedals
controls.text: Pushing the left or right pedal moves the rudder and turns the nose during the landing glide.
controls.context: On the real flight the computer landed Buran by itself on the runway at Baikonur.
